newsitem.title: GERMANY: Ship sails into German storm over US genetic soy.
newsitem.headline: Ship sails into German storm over US genetic soy.

text.p: A ship due to dock at Hamburg late on Tuesday with a cargo of soyabeans may carry the first genetically-altered US soybeans to be exported to Europe where environmentalists are set to whip up a new wave of protest.
Health anxieties about biotechnology are most acute in Germany where the Greenpeace lobby group leads a campaign against the modified soya.
Developed by chemicals giant Monsanto of the United States, it has been altered to resist a widely-used weedkiller.
Interest on Tuesday centred on the inbound freighter Ideal Progress with 44,600 tonnes of new crop soybeans aboard shipped for Oelmuehle Hamburg (Oelag), a leading European processor.
"Production schedules have not been altered," said Arnd von Wissel, board head at the firm. "There are customers waiting for the products."
As some one to two percent of the US soyabean crop is now made up of genetically-altered beans, environmentalists say it is likely that some of this material is aboard Ideal Progress.
The campaigners want the food industry to boycott these beans or at least label products to tell consumers that they might have been derived from genetically-altered organisms.
Soya is used in some form or another in some 30,000 foodstuffs including margarine, chocolate or mayonnaise.

Some leading food firms including the German unit of Anglo-Dutch Unilever have responded to Germnan consumer concerns and say they won't sell products containing oils from modified beans, although they consider them safe.

Dutch food group Nutricia said last week it would not use genetically-altered soybeans in infant milk formulas. Spokesman Klaas De Jong said his firm was happy about tests that had been done on the beans but "the client is king".
The German VDO crushers' organization sees what an official called "a short-term reaction to consumer concerns".
"It does not mean that processors doubt the safety of the new beans or that they are negative towards the use of biotechnology in food production," he said.

With the US new crop in full swing, soybean ships are expected in Hamburg at 10-day intervals over the next few months. Other vessels carrying soy are due in Antwerp. The United States last year sold an estimated two million tonnes to Germany worth $690 million and accounting for two-thirds of German imports of soybeans.

Sunseed and rapeseed can be used instead of soya but traders dopubt if Germans can isolate themselves, and say that the use of biotechnology cannot be stopped. Argentina is another big supplier and it plans to use modified seeds in 1997.
